My family has farmed this land for two decades. I know Quzhou's soils — alkaline, sandy-loamy, prone to drought in spring. The wheat-maize rotation is my bread and butter. Cotton is harder work but brings in more cash, which we need since my husband and oldest child work in town and can't always help at planting and harvest.

My 13.1 mu splits naturally: 8 mu in the wheat-maize rotation, 5.1 mu in cotton. The same 8 mu grows wheat in winter and maize in summer — that's how we do it here. The cotton plot stays cotton.

For **winter wheat**, I'll stick with the improved variety from the township supply station — I've used it three years running and it's reliable. Four irrigations: winter water in November, jointing in April, heading in May, and one at grain fill if it's dry. I apply base fertilizer before seeding and topdress at jointing. Two pesticide sprays — one herbicide in winter, one fungicide before heading.

For **summer maize**, I go straight hybrid seed, no question. After wheat harvest in June, I'll no-till direct seed. It saves me labor and the soil stays moist. Two irrigations if summer rain is light. Two pesticide passes.

For **cotton**, I plough deep in March before transplanting. Cotton takes the most out of me — six pesticide applications through the season for bollworm, aphids, red spider mite. Four irrigations spaced through July and August. I use a hybrid Bt cotton to keep bollworm pressure down some, but I still spray.
